title: EgoLens: Teachable Driving-Data Viewer
pitch: Agents don't just use EgoLens, they extend it. Drop an unknown driving dataset: your agent writes the adapter, you judge the 3D render. Each does what it's best at, and the viewer keeps growing.
about_excerpt: Agents don't just use EgoLens, they extend it. Drop an unknown driving dataset: your agent writes the adapter, you judge the 3D render. Each does what it's best at, and the viewer keeps growing. Like Comment Story Updates Unknown dataset detected Teaching new dataset format New dataset learned! dataset rendered Inspiration Every perception team has sensor data in a shape no viewer understands: a research dataset, or their own model output stored next to one. Someone writes a loader, debugs why the point cloud renders sideways, and the loader dies with the notebook. EgoLens already renders Waymo, nuScenes, and Argoverse 2 in the browser, and every new format still meant a hand-written adapter. WebMCP changes who can add one: your agent teaches EgoLens through WebMCP, you approve the render, and the app's capabilities keep growing. What it does WebMCP tools usually let agents use the app. EgoLens flips it: agents extend the app. Together, a person and an agent can now add a dataset format to a viewer in minutes, in the browser, without touching the source code. Drop a folder EgoLens does not recognize and the page becomes a WebMCP tool provider. The agent inspects files within strict byte limits, reads the recipe schema and operator vocabulary, and submits adapter recipes as declarative JSON, never code. Every validated revision renders in the production 3D viewer, docked next to the review panel : orbit, scrub the timeline, toggle boxes and segmentation, switch camera POVs. You accept or reject each capability with a named issue and the verdict flows back to the agent. Finalize seals the recipe with content hashes; it can be exported, imported, and shared. Every taught format stays: drop that layout again and it renders in one click. The app's capabilities keep growing, and files never leave the browser. How we built it Five tools registered on document.modelContext : inspect , get_contract , apply_revision , get_state , finalize . Self-describing descriptions, normalized inputs, string results, so ChatGPT's browser, Chrome's native WebMCP, and the Codex app drive them with zero agent-specific code. Recipes are data, executed in an isolated graph runtime with resource limits. The person confirms the sensor layout before teaching starts; a recipe that does not bind exactly those sensors is rejected. React 19, TypeScript, three.js, Web Workers, IndexedDB, GitHub Pages. 1,100 unit tests and Playwright probes that drive Chrome's real WebMCP end to end. Challenges we ran into Agents stopping at the timeline. Fixed without shipping any dataset example, which would leak the answer: a sensor contract, coverage diagnostics, and a next-step hint in every state read. Bugs only eyes can catch. PandaSet stores cuboid yaw along the width axis. Every automated check passed and the boxes were rotated 90° on screen. That is why the full renderer is the review surface. Host budgets. Codex caps descriptor size and call latency; in-app browsers hang on the File System Access API. Each constraint pushed the tool surface toward the plainest contract. Accomplishments that we're proud of Three unknown datasets taught end to end by agents in one week: A2D2 (3 revisions, 6 cameras + 6 LiDARs fused), KITTI Raw (7 revisions), PandaSet (world-frame poses, pandas pickles). No example recipe is ever shown to the agent. The same five tools work unchanged across three hosts, and each dataset taught left EgoLens able to read more than before. What we learned The interesting question is not "what can an agent do in my app" but "what can an agent make my app able to do". Expose the extension points as tools and the agent's output becomes an artifact a person can inspect, reject, seal, and share. The person's rejections were the most valuable signal in the loop. What's next for EgoLens: Teachable Driving-Data Viewer A public recipe registry. A student or a researcher teaches EgoLens the dataset they need and publishes the recipe, so it renders for everyone after that. The goal: a visualization tool that can read any AV dataset, taught by the people who use it. video_transcript_excerpt: Ego Lens is a browser based explorer for autonomous driving data. An hour ago, it did not support this data set. No one wrote code for it. An agent taught the viewer to read it through web MCP tools on this page. I, the human, reviewed every rendered revision until it was right and approved it. Here's how. Ego Lens is a browser tool people use because it just works. Drop a driving data set in and it renders. No pre-processing, no install. But today, I need to render a data set it has never seen. I open Codex in app browser and drop the sample log. Instead of rendering, the page opens a teaching screen. I name the data set, confirm the six cameras and one lidar it detected, and the page tells me the one sentence to say to Codex agent, "Teach Ego Lens this data set." So, Codex starts calling the web MCP tools this page exposes. It reads samples of the files, figures out what a recipe needs to look like, and submits one. Every step is a tool call. Ego Lens's job here is to validate that recipe, and once it passes, render it. Then I, the human, take a look at the render, and if something's off, I tell Codex exactly what's wrong so it can try again. Like right now, when we hit play, the car in the center stays put, but the point cloud around it, the rings that should be spreading out from that car, drifts forward on its own. They should move together. No automated check catches that, but a person sees it in 2 seconds. So, I just type what I see. Ego pose seems detached from the lidar and 3D boxes. That's all Codex needs. A minute later, a new revision comes in. Let me play it again. Now, the point cloud and the car move together, the boxes sit on the vehicles, and the cameras line up. Everything looks right. So, I go through the list and approve each one. Timeline, poses, point cloud, cameras, boxes, projection, segmentation. Then I finalize and Ego Lens seals the recipe. That's it. Ego Lens can now read a data set it had never seen before. Now, watch what happens when I drop the same folder again. No teaching this time. Ego Lens recognizes the format, matches it to the recipe it just sealed, and renders right away. And that works for any other log in this data set, too. And because a recipe is just a JSON file, I can host it right next to the data and pack both into a single link. Whoever taught the data set to Eagle lens shares that link, and whoever opens it gets the whole scene. That's where this is going. A public registry of recipes, so once someone teaches Eagle lens a format, it renders for everyone after that. Any data set, not just three. And your own data never has to leave your machine.

live_observation.first_impression: EgoLens presents a driving-data viewer with Waymo, nuScenes, and Argoverse 2 options, hosted dataset shortcuts, and a custom dataset URL loader.
live_observation.after_state: The dataset selector changed to nuScenes and the URL populated with https://data.egolens.org/nuscenes/, enabling Load, but no rendered scene appeared in the observed state.
live_observation.notes: The viewer's supported-format workflow is clearly exposed; the shortcut did not itself show a render within the wait.
